name: glTF
licence: Other (Khronos Group specification licence, no SPDX id — see repo LICENSE.md; permissive for implementers, attribution required for spec text reuse)
size_note: ~252 MB full-history clone (spec text + schema + figures); shallow clone at pinned SHA is a few MB
why: Authoritative normative text and JSON schema for glTF 2.0 (ISO/IEC 12113:2022) — read the schema/ directory to see the exact node/mesh/material/animation object definitions your exporter and runtime loader must agree on.

name: glTF-Sample-Assets
licence: Mixed per-asset (CC0/CC-BY/CC-BY-SA — see each model's own license.txt; no single repo-wide licence, code samples untagged on GitHub)
size_note: ~1.67 GB full history — LARGE, avoid full clone; use --small mode or sparse-checkout a handful of models
why: The canonical corpus of feature-test glTF files (morph targets, skinning, KTX2 textures, sparse accessors) used by every engine's conformance suite — pull individual models with sparse checkout to validate your loader against edge cases, not the whole repo.

name: glTF-Sample-Viewer
size_note: ~877 MB full history (includes submodule assets); shallow clone of code only is small
why: Khronos' reference WebGL2 PBR renderer — study its shader implementation of the metallic-roughness BRDF to sanity-check your own renderer's material output against the spec-sanctioned rendering.

name: glTF-Validator
size_note: ~4.6 MB — small, safe to always clone
why: Command-line and browser-based conformance checker for glTF/.glb files — wire this into your CI asset pipeline so any exported .glb is rejected before it reaches the runtime if it violates the spec.

name: KTX-Software
licence: Apache-2.0 (with bundled third-party components under their own permissive licences — see LICENSE.md for the full list)
size_note: ~325 MB full history; ktx2ktx2/toktx binaries are the practical deliverable, not the full source tree
why: Reference implementation of the KTX2 container plus toktx/ktx2check CLI tools — use these to pre-compress textures to Basis Universal/UASTC before packing them into your .glb so browser memory stays within budget.

name: glTF-Blender-IO
size_note: ~49 MB full history — small, safe to always clone
why: The actual Blender add-on source (now bundled in Blender core) that performs the DCC-to-glTF export — read io_scene_gltf2/blender/exp to understand exactly which Blender material/armature features map cleanly to glTF and which get silently dropped.

name: three.js
size_note: ~1.6 GB full history (examples + docs); a shallow clone of the tag is far smaller (~150-200 MB, mostly example assets)
why: Study examples/jsm/loaders/GLTFLoader.js as a second, independent implementation of glTF parsing to cross-check the Sample-Viewer's interpretation, and examples/webgl_* for WebGL2 renderer-state patterns.

name: Babylon.js
size_note: ~1.4 GB full history; shallow clone of the tag is smaller but still large due to bundled playground assets
why: Babylon's packages/dev/core/src/Loading/glTF loader and its built-in scene-optimizer are a useful contrast to three.js for camera rig and LOD/scene-budget patterns aimed at a similar browser target.

name: PlayCanvas engine
size_note: ~624 MB full history; shallow clone of the tag is considerably smaller
why: A third WebGL2/WebGPU engine with a leaner core than Babylon — read src/scene/graph-node.js for a minimal, production-grade scene-graph implementation to benchmark your own engine's node-transform propagation against.

name: godot-demo-projects (3d/platformer)
size_note: ~485 MB full history for the whole monorepo; the 3d/platformer subfolder alone is a few MB (use sparse-checkout)
why: Official third-person/platformer demo (3d/platformer) showing Godot's CharacterBody3D movement and a follow-camera rig — the direct authoring-side analogue of the camera-relative movement and camera rig you must replicate at runtime.

name: godot-demo-projects (3d/rigidbody_character & kinematic_character)
size_note: shared clone with REF-10 — sparse-checkout only these two subfolders to keep it under a few MB
why: Contrasts a physics-driven (RigidBody3D) vs. kinematic (CharacterBody3D) third-person controller in the same engine version, clarifying which movement model to standardise on for a fixed-tick simulation.

name: Godot engine (4.7.1-stable)
size_note: ~1.8 GB full history; shallow clone of the tag (source only, no build artifacts) is roughly 300-400 MB
why: Pin the exact engine source tag your team is authoring against so glTF export behaviour, GLES3/Vulkan-to-WebGL2 rendering differences, and web-export template builds are all reproducible from a known commit.

name: Godot: Exporting for the Web
ref: stable (docs branch, not versioned by tag)
why: Official documentation of the exact COOP/COEP response headers (Cross-Origin-Opener-Policy: same-origin, Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy: require-corp) required for threaded WebAssembly builds — mandatory reading before choosing your hosting configuration.

name: MDN: Cross-Origin-Embedder-Policy
ref: current (MDN is continuously updated, no version tag)
why: Explains precisely why COEP/COOP headers gate access to SharedArrayBuffer and postMessage-based multithreading in the browser — the underlying platform rule that Godot's web-export threading requirement is built on.

name: WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation)
ref: W3C Recommendation, 12 December 2024 (also ratified as ISO/IEC 40500:2025)
licence: W3C Document Licence (free to read/cite; redistribution/modification restricted)
why: The normative accessibility success-criteria checklist (contrast, focus visibility, target size, motion) to audit your game's HUD/menu layer against, since WCAG 2.2 was ISO-ratified in October 2025 and is the current baseline auditors will cite.

name: Godot: Internationalizing games
ref: stable (docs branch, not versioned by tag)
why: Concrete i18n approach for a Godot-authored game: locale-vs-language distinction, CSV/PO translation import, pluralisation and pseudolocalisation testing workflow to adopt for the desktop authoring lane before export.

name: Poly Haven
ref: n/a (asset library, not a git repo; licence page checked live)
licence: CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain) for every HDRI, texture, and 3D model on the site
size_note: per-asset download, no bulk clone; glTF/.glb exports available directly from the site for many models
why: Zero-restriction, zero-attribution PBR textures and props already exported in glTF/.glb — use for environment dressing so no asset-licence audit is ever needed for these files.

name: Kenney game assets
ref: n/a (asset library, not a single git repo; licence checked per-pack on site)
licence: CC0 1.0 Universal (public domain) on essentially all packs — verify per-pack page since a small number of bundled fonts carry their own separate licence
size_note: per-pack ZIP download, no bulk clone
why: Large catalogue of stylised low-poly 3D model packs and UI kits with unambiguous CC0 terms, well suited for prototyping an educational game's props and interface before commissioning bespoke art.

name: ISO/IEC 12113:2022 (glTF, ISO reference record)
ref: n/a (ISO catalogue record, no git ref)
licence: ISO copyright — the ISO catalogue page is free to view; the full ISO-formatted PDF is normally paywalled, use the free Khronos-hosted GitHub spec (REF-01) as the working copy of identical normative text
why: Confirms glTF 2.0's formal identity as ISO/IEC 12113:2022 for procurement or compliance documentation, even though day-to-day engineering should reference the freely available Khronos GitHub spec text instead.
